{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"# The server was part of the appliance.

When you bought your connected lock, thermostat, camera, light, speaker, or oven, the server wasn’t printed on the box as a separate appliance. It was still part of the appliance. The physical object in your home was one component; the vendor’s cloud service was another. I use “appliance” here to mean the whole thing you were sold (device, app, account, and remote computers), because that whole system performed the advertised job.

Then the vendor closes the service. Perhaps the hardware still powers on. Perhaps a button still works. But you’ve lost remote access, schedules, notifications, voice control, shared accounts, automation, history, security updates, or even the ability to finish setup. Which features disappear depends on the design, but the governing fact doesn’t: if your device must ask a distant server for permission or instructions, you can’t keep the complete product running by keeping the box. The sale – as you understood it – has been partially reversed.

What’s the vendor likely to say? The device remains yours; only an online service has ended. That distinction is tidy, and it’s bullshit. If the promised function required the server on the day of sale, the server was part of the function. I call this the removable-appliance trick: sell you a machine, retain one essential gear in somebody else’s building, then announce that you still own everything because the shell remains on your counter.

Of course, no company can promise to operate forever. Servers cost money, businesses fail, security standards change, and old systems become dangerous. But that concession doesn’t settle who should bear the cost of shutdown. Why should you absorb the entire loss when the vendor chose an architecture that made your purchase dependent on its continued cooperation? I don’t expect immortality from a cloud service. I expect an exit that respects the original bargain (not merely the vendor’s cheapest escape).

When we buy durable goods for our homes, all of us rely on a plain market expectation: ownership should outlast the seller’s enthusiasm. We should carry that expectation into connected devices, because we’re otherwise accepting a peculiar kind of tenancy. You pay the purchase price, supply the electricity, maintain the network, and accept the physical risk – but the vendor keeps a remote fuse box. When it leaves, it pulls the fuse. That isn’t a normal appliance sale; it’s a lease whose termination clause was hidden in the wiring.

Local operation changes the balance. A locally operable device can perform its core functions on your network without consulting the vendor: a lock can lock, a thermostat can follow a schedule, a camera can record to storage you control, and a switch can respond to local automation. The cloud may add convenience (remote access while you’re away), but it shouldn’t hold the core function hostage. If the service closes, you lose an accessory rather than the machine – the difference between a broken bonus and a bricked purchase.

Local operation also protects your choices before shutdown. You can keep using a device when the vendor changes an app, raises a fee, removes an integration, or decides that your perfectly functional hardware is “legacy.” I’ve no quarrel with vendors selling optional hosting, backups, or remote relay services. The problem starts when those services become compulsory control points. A dependency you can decline is a feature; a dependency you can’t escape is leverage (and the leverage belongs to the seller).

The practical demand is simple. Core functions should work locally, setup shouldn’t require a cloud account, and vendors should document local interfaces. If remote servers are essential, buyers deserve a shutdown plan that unlocks local control, releases the necessary software, or provides a credible transition period. My point isn’t that every feature must survive every business failure. It’s that the seller shouldn’t design failure so the buyer’s property fails with it.

A connected appliance has two bodies: the object in your hand and the service somewhere else. The sales pitch includes both, so the shutdown bargain must account for both. Let vendors close their servers when they must, but make them leave the appliance behind. The server was part of the appliance; local operation is how you keep the appliance when the server is gone.","omitted":[{"habit":"opponents-allies-sources / o12","why":"The request supplies no named vendor, verified source, or attributed shutdown language to credit and test."}],"refused":""}
